newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: BONDS CRACKDOWN TO SAVE BILLIONS
Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, has announced the Government is moving to close a loophole which would have cost four billion dollars in lost taxation revenue.
Mr Costello says the Government will introduce legislation to change the infrastructure bonds scheme to block proposals that are aimed at minimising tax.
He says there were 12 projects accepted under the scheme between its introduction in 1994 and July 1996.
But 71 applications were received in July and August 1996. He describes some of them as extremely tax aggressive.
TREASURER PRAISES LENDER FOR HOME LOAN RATES SQUEEZE
The federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, has praised a new player in the mortgage market, Aussie Home Loans, for kicking off home loan interest rate cuts among the major banks.
He says he hopes the company succeeds in starting a similar squeeze in relation to business lending.
Mr Costello also welcomed the National Australia Bank cutting its interest rates to match the Commonwealth Bank cuts on standard variable loans.
The NAB is the first major bank to respond to the Commonwealth's challenge.
The rate falls to seven-point-five-five per cent and will apply from next Monday for new customers, and from April for existing ones.
EUTHANASIA OPPONENT SLAMS REPORT
Northern Territory anti-euthanasia campaigner, Chris Wake, has disputed the findings of a study, showing a-third of all deaths in Australia are hastened by a doctor.
Authors of the report, to be published in the Medical Journal of Australia, say the findings suggest the law hasn't prevented the practice of euthanasia.
But Dr Wake says the true incidence of euthanasia is really around one per cent.
He says the report has expanded the definition of euthanasia across all end-of-life decisions.
INDUSTRIAL ACTION ANGERS CUSTOMS
The Australian Customs Service says industrial action at Sydney Airport over the past two days has potential serious consequences for Australian border security.

Customs and the Public Sector Union are in the Industrial Commission after stoppages by Customs officials prevented detailed inspection of five-thousand passengers who arrived at Sydney airport in the past two days.
The Public Sector Union is angry at Customs moves to introduce extensive part-time work at Sydney Airport.
Customs advertised at the weekend for more than 130 part-time staff.
The union says this goes well beyond numbers allowed in an agreement on part-time work.
Customs has requested the Industrial Relations Commission issue orders against any further industrial action over the matter.
JOHN HOWARD DIFFICULT TO WORK WITH, SAYS YUNUPINGU
The chair of the Northern Land Council says John Howard, compared with other Prime Ministers, is very slow, reluctant and always tricking people around.
Gallarwuy Yunupingu helped launch a book in Canberra this week on 20 years of land rights.
He's been chair of the land council for 18 of the past 20 years, and worked with four Prime Ministers.
Mr Yunupingu says John Howard is the most difficult Prime Minister he's had to work with on Aboriginal affairs.
MOORE UNSURPRISED BY EUTHANASIA FINDINGS
ACT Independent MLA, Michael Moore, says he's not surprised a survey has found a third of all Australian deaths come about through medical decisions intended to hasten a patient's death.

Mr Moore is to introduce euthanasia legislation next week, and it's thought the law could be passed with a majority of one. The survey of three-thousand doctors found deaths came from doctors prescribing or administering lethal drugs with or without a patient's consent, or by with-holding of treatment.
Mr Moore hopes the survey will encourage the Australian Medical Association to rethink its stance on voluntary euthanasia.
TRIAL ABORTED AFTER TV REPORT
A Supreme Court murder trial in Sydney has been aborted due to a television report of the legal proceedings.

Twenty-seven year old David John Zammitt was standing trial, charged with the murder and armed robbery of Toula Soravia while she was banking money from the family service station at Summer Hill in 1994.
Justice Peter Newman today discharged the jury and has referred the matter to the New South Wales Attorney-General's office.
The abrupt end to the trial, which was due to last several weeks, followed a report on Channel Ten news about what happened in the courtroom yesterday in the jury's absence.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
